intro: The Qur'an is a short book. In most printed copies it runs to about 600 pages, and a trained reciter can finish it in a day and a night. Yet Muslims have been reading it for fourteen centuries, and the books written to explain it fill libraries. This unit asks how that reading happens: who does it, what tools they use, and why careful readers can look at the same verse and see different things.

The first chapter follows the tradition of interpretation. You will meet the hadith, the reports about the Prophet, and the scholars who sifted them. You will open the great commentaries of al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, learn what the Qur'an itself says about clear and ambiguous verses, and see how Sunni, Shia and Sufi readers each approach the text. The second chapter follows the book out into the world: into art, science, schools and law, into Persian and Swahili and Malay, into Latin and English, and finally into America, in the memory of enslaved scholars and in the mosques of Chicago today.

By the end you will be able to explain what a hadith is and how it was tested, describe how a commentary works, name the main groups of readers and how they differ, trace the Qur'an's path into other languages and lands, and tell the story of the Qur'an in America with names and dates. Above all, you will be able to say, of any claim about what the Qur'an means, "That is how this reader reads it," and know how to find out why.
bigQuestion: Who gets to say what the Qur'an means, and how has one Arabic book shaped so many languages, arts and lands?

timeline.t: Muhammad dies in Medina; Muslims begin gathering reports of his words and deeds
Sibawayh of Basra dies, leaving the first full grammar of Arabic
The caliph al-Ma'mun supports translators and scholars in Baghdad, the House of Wisdom
Al-Bukhari dies; his Sahih becomes the most trusted Sunni hadith collection
Al-Tabari dies in Baghdad; his tafsir gathers the readings of three centuries
The Nizamiyya madrasa opens in Baghdad, a model school for the Qur'an and law
Robert of Ketton finishes the first Latin translation of the Qur'an in Spain
Ibn Kathir dies in Damascus; his tafsir is still widely read
George Sale publishes the first English Qur'an made directly from Arabic
Omar ibn Said, enslaved in North Carolina, writes his life in Arabic, opening with Surah 67
The World's Parliament of Religions meets in Chicago; Islam is presented to an American audience
Marmaduke Pickthall publishes The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, this course's text

words.d: a report of what Muhammad said, did or approved, passed down through a chain of narrators
the chain of names showing who passed a hadith down
the Prophet's way of living, taken by Muslims as a model and known through the hadith
commentary that explains the Qur'an, often verse by verse
a clear verse, which 3:7 calls the foundation of the Book
an ambiguous verse, whose meaning is uncertain or has more than one sense
abrogation; the debated idea that a later verse replaces an earlier ruling
Islam's trained religious scholars, who teach, debate and give opinions
a school of Islamic law; four main Sunni schools and the Shia Ja'fari school
the art of beautiful writing, the main religious art of the Muslim world
the direction of Mecca, which Muslims face in prayer and which a mosque's mihrab marks
a school for Qur'an, hadith, grammar and Islamic law

test.q: What are the two parts of a hadith?
test.why: A hadith has a chain of narrators, the isnad, and a text, the matn.

test.q: What did al-Bukhari and Muslim do in the 800s?
choices: Founded the four schools of law
Sifted huge numbers of reports and kept those they judged sound
test.why: Each compiled a Sahih, a collection of reports judged sound after checking their chains.

test.q: How does the Sunnah relate to the Qur'an for most Muslims?
choices: It is part of the Qur'an
It is a translation of the Qur'an
It is the second source of guidance, showing how the Prophet lived the Qur'an
test.why: The Qur'an comes first; the Sunnah, known through hadith, fills in what the Qur'an states briefly.

test.q: What was al-Tabari's method in his tafsir?
choices: Gathering earlier readings with their chains, then judging which was strongest
test.why: Al-Tabari (d. 923) collected reports on each verse and then stated which reading he found strongest.

test.q: Which commentator's first step is to explain a verse with other verses of the Qur'an?
test.why: Ibn Kathir (d. 1373) is known for the method "the Qur'an explains the Qur'an," followed by hadith.

test.q: Why can Surah 3:7 be read two ways?
choices: The place where the reader pauses changes the meaning
test.why: The Arabic words are the same; stopping at different points gives two meanings about who knows the ambiguous verses.

test.q: How do most classical and modern scholars read 9:5 in relation to 2:256, "no compulsion in religion"?
choices: The two verses say the same thing
9:5 is tied to a specific broken treaty, and 2:256 still stands
test.why: Mainstream scholars read 9:5 in its context and hold that 2:256 remains in force; a minority of medieval jurists argued otherwise.

test.q: For Shia Muslims, who are the guided interpreters of the Qur'an?
choices: The Imams from the Prophet's family
The collectors of the Six Books
test.why: Shia Muslims hold that leadership and interpretation passed through Ali's family, the Imams.

test.q: What do Sufi readers look for beneath the plain sense of a verse?
test.why: Sufis such as al-Qushayri and al-Ghazali sought the batin, while holding that the zahir still stands.

test.q: Why do the Sunni schools of law differ on details?
choices: Each was founded in a different century
They weigh the sources, such as hadith and analogy, differently
test.why: The four schools share the same sources and rank them differently, so rulings differ on details.

test.q: Which languages were written in the Arabic alphabet as Islam spread?
test.why: The Qur'an's alphabet traveled with the book into many languages of Muslim peoples.

test.q: What religious needs helped drive Muslim astronomy?
choices: The lunar calendar, prayer times and the direction of Mecca
test.why: Ramadan and the pilgrimage follow the moon, prayer follows the sun, and mosques must face Mecca.

test.q: Who commissioned the first Latin translation of the Qur'an in 1143?
choices: Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny
test.why: Peter the Venerable paid Robert of Ketton to make the Latin version so Christians could read and argue with it.

test.q: Why does this course quote Pickthall's 1930 translation?
choices: It is the only English translation
It was made by a non-Muslim
It is in the public domain in the United States
test.why: Pickthall's text may be quoted freely; later translations such as Yusuf Ali's are under copyright.

test.q: What did Omar ibn Said write in 1831?
choices: A translation of the Qur'an into English
His life story in Arabic, opening with Surah 67
test.why: Omar ibn Said, enslaved in North Carolina, wrote his life in Arabic and began with Surah Al-Mulk; the Library of Congress holds it.

write.prompt: Can two careful readers disagree about a verse of the Qur'an and both be following the tradition? Choose one verse from this unit (for example 3:7, 2:238, 5:6 or 2:106) and cite it by surah and ayah. Use at least two named readers (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, a Shia or Sufi commentator, or a translator). Explain what the verse says, how each reader reads it and what tools each uses.
tips: Cite each passage by surah and ayah, and name the translation you use.
Attribute every reading to its reader: "al-Tabari reads this as…", "Shia commentators hold…"
Describe how the readers differ and why; do not decide who is right.
Use the unit's terms: isnad, tafsir, muhkam, mutashabih, naskh, madhhab.
Keep each paragraph to one idea, and end by saying what the disagreement shows about how the Qur'an is read.
